Nether means lower or situated further down, particularly when referring to something beneath the surface, underground, or at the bottom of something. Think of it as the opposite of "upper." If something is in the nether part of a place, it is in the deeper, lower, or more hidden part of it.

That's the core. But this word has a personality — it doesn't get used for just anything that is "low." It carries a sense of depth, darkness, and hiddenness. It tends to describe places or regions that are beneath the known, visible world — places that are somewhat mysterious, unseen, or far removed from the ordinary surface of things. This is what makes it feel more powerful and evocative than simply saying "lower."
The Three Key Ways It Is Used

1. Physically lower or beneath the surface

This is its most literal use. If you are exploring a cave and someone mentions "the nether regions of the cave," they mean the deepest, lowest parts — the sections far down below, hidden from light and easy reach. Similarly, "the nether depths of the ocean" refers to the very bottom, the dark and unreachable deep. You can use it for anything that sits at the bottom or lower portion of a physical space.

2. The underworld, hell, or the realm of the dead

This is where the word gets its most famous and literary use. "The nether world" or "the nether realm" refers to the underworld — the place below the earth where, in mythology, religion, and literature, the dead reside. It is used to describe hell, the afterlife beneath the ground, or any dark spiritual dimension "below" our world. When poets, authors, or religious texts speak of descending into darkness and death, they often reach for "nether." It fits perfectly because the underworld is, by nature, beneath everything — lower than the living world. This gives the word a somewhat eerie, solemn, and dramatic feeling.

3. A polite, indirect reference to the lower body

In everyday, informal use, "nether regions" or "nether parts" is a common and gently humorous euphemism for the genitals or the area of the body below the waist. It's a way of referring to private body parts without being crude or clinical. Doctors, comedians, and ordinary people alike use this phrase when they want to speak about that area with a touch of delicacy or lighthearted indirectness.
The Phrase You Will Encounter Most

The single most common combination you will meet is "nether regions." This phrase does a lot of heavy lifting because it covers all three uses above depending on the context — the deep lower parts of a physical place, the underworld, or the lower body. Pay attention to the surrounding context, and the meaning will always be clear.
The Feeling and Register of the Word

"Nether" is not a word of everyday casual conversation. It is literary, slightly old-fashioned, and formal in tone. You are far more likely to encounter it in novels, poetry, mythology, religious texts, fantasy writing, or deliberate humor than in a simple chat between friends. When a writer chooses "nether" over "lower" or "beneath," they are making a conscious choice to add weight, atmosphere, or a hint of the dramatic and the dark to their writing.

It is not a dead or obsolete word, though. It is alive and well — you will still encounter it regularly in reading, and it is completely understood by native speakers. It simply lives in a more elevated, intentional register of language.
How It Differs from Similar Words

"Lower," "beneath," and "under" are its plain, everyday cousins. They describe position without any special feeling. "Nether" does the same job but wraps that position in an atmosphere of depth, obscurity, and often darkness. Choosing "nether" signals that the lower place in question is not merely physically below — it is somehow removed from the familiar, the bright, or the ordinary.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

"Nether" means lower, further beneath the surface, or belonging to a deep and often dark or hidden realm. It is used literally for the deep lower parts of places, mythologically for the underworld and hell, and colloquially as a polite way to refer to the lower parts of the human body. Its tone is literary, slightly archaic, and evocative — always pointing downward, always suggesting something beneath the visible world.
